title: Verifier-Gated LLM NetOps: A Preregistered Artifact-Backed Evaluation of Input Sanitization and Deterministic Verification
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study_id cand-2026-03) that measured whether template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating (and at-most-one automated repair) changes the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents. The frozen run used the declared generator gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within an orchestration adapter. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; complete paired outcomes used in the primary analysis = 141. Observed per-pair acceptance: Baseline 135/141 (95.7447%); Guarded 141/141 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.04255319148936165; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. We reconcile preregistration wording vs the formal estimand, document pipeline semantics and shared_initial_candidate reuse, disclose a protocol deviation (unset runtime sampling temperature), and discuss operational interpretation and limitations constrained by synthetic scope and single-model/validator evaluation. All principal numeric claims are supported by the archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest [14]).

sections.introduction:
Automating network operations (NetOps) by translating high-level operator intent into device CLI with large language models (LLMs) promises reduced toil and faster change delivery, but also introduces risks: syntactic errors, ordering mistakes, and violations of deployment invariants that deterministic validators would flag as unsafe. Deterministic validators that reason about configuration effects (reachability, required sequencing, protected interfaces) are natural deployment gates, yet prior LLM–NetOps evaluations frequently rely on surface metrics (token overlap, edit distance) that do not measure deployability or acceptance by a semantics-oriented validator [3,8,9].

This study asks a narrow, operational estimand amenable to preregistered inference: does template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair change the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI under adversarially mutated intents? The experiment (cand-2026-03) was preregistered and executed end-to-end under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics so that each Baseline–Guarded pair compares validator outcomes after applying only downstream guarded-pipeline operations (sanitization, gating, permitted repair) to a single shared LLM draft. The work contributes: (1) a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment executed end-to-end; (2) an explicit, artifact-grounded description of per-condition pipeline semantics and shared_initial_candidate reuse; (3) confirmatory quantitative results on a synthetic adversarial bank showing a small but statistically detectable absolute change in validator acceptance; and (4) reconciliation of preregistration natural-language hypothesis wording with the formal estimand plus disclosure of a protocol deviation (unset sampling temperature).
sections.related_work:
Deterministic network-verification tools provide the technical basis for validator-centred gating. Header Space Analysis, VeriFlow and NetPlumber-style systems check forwarding and policy invariants over explicit network models and report property-level violations rather than surface mismatches, making them suitable deployment gates for generated configurations while still limited by the expressiveness of encoded invariants [5–7,14].

Empirical studies of LLMs for configuration synthesis (e.g., NetConfEval, NetLLMBench) consistently show that model-only generation produces both syntactic and higher-level semantic errors (ordering, precondition violations, protected-interface breaches) and that surface-match metrics correlate poorly with deployability measured by deterministic validators [3,8,9]. Generate–validate–repair architectures, where an LLM draft is checked by tools and then repaired using precise verifier feedback, have been shown in prototype work to improve concrete outcome metrics when repair scope is bounded and verifier diagnostics are precise, but these demonstrations remain prototype-scale and often require human oversight [11,3,32].

Security-oriented work documents prompt-injection and indirect prompt attacks that can subvert LLM-integrated pipelines, motivating defenses such as slot validation, input sanitization, and strict gating policies; rigorous NetOps-specific threat modelling and defensive evaluation remain open research areas [10,49]. Benchmarking efforts argue for validator-centred, operational metrics (deployability, safety) rather than lexical similarity alone; our preregistered estimand adopts that operational stance by using deterministic-validator acceptance as the primary quantity of interest [4,9].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. Study cand-2026-03 was preregistered before outcome observation; the primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: for each adversarial intent generate a single shared_initial_candidate and record a binary outcome indicating whether the deterministic validator would accept the final candidate for deployment. The preregistered confirmatory test was the exact two-sided McNemar; bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729.

Design, scope, and adversary model. The preregistration specified N = 150 adversarial intents (paired episodes across Baseline and Guarded) drawn from synthetic templates exercising interface admin changes, MTU/VLAN updates, required sequences (shutdown–change–restore patterns), and protected-interface rules. The adversary applied deterministic mutation heuristics to these templates. Scope is limited to the supplied synthetic templates and the deterministic CLI grammar encoded in the validator; no production data were used.

Models, validator, and orchestration. The declared generator was gpt-5-mini and the deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The orchestration adapter implemented two conditions: Baseline (validator applied directly to the shared_initial_candidate) and Guarded (template-based sanitizer applied, deterministic gating enforced, and at-most-one automated repair permitted). The archived model configuration recorded declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset); this unset sampling parameter is disclosed as a protocol deviation (see Disclosure Statement).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and per-pair timeline. Because generation semantics were preregistered as shared_initial_candidate, each paired episode followed: (1) task instantiation and adversarial mutation; (2) single LLM call producing the shared_initial_candidate (one draft reused by both conditions); (3) Baseline scoring: validator applied to the shared draft; (4) Guarded branch: sanitizer applied and, if the policy permitted, at-most-one repair LLM call was allowed; (5) final validation of the sanitized or repaired candidate and recording of the guarded decision. This design isolates downstream guarded-pipeline effects as the causal factors under test; only downstream validation/repair can create paired outcome differences.

Missingness, exclusions, and operational counts. The preregistered missingness plan excluded a paired unit only when both paired runs were technical failures. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 300, completed_episode_count = 282, failed_episode_count = 18, and complete_pair_count = 141 after applying the exclusion rule. Provider-call accounting and stage counts in the reconciliation artifact report model_calls_used = 156 total hosted model-call events (147 completed, 9 failed), stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 6. Primary analysis used the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1 implementation (exact McNemar) and the bootstrap parameters noted above; all analysis inputs and parameters are archived in the execution manifest [14].

Statistical procedures. The primary confirmatory test is the exact two-sided McNemar on the paired 2×2 contingency table (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00 computed over complete pairs). The paired point estimate reported is the empirical difference in marginal success rates (guarded − baseline). Confidence intervals are bootstrap percentile intervals computed by resampling paired units with replacement (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Sensitivity analyses included a conservative treatment of excluded both-missing pairs as failures (reported in Results).
sections.results:
Execution and raw counts. The run completed 282 of 300 planned episodes; 18 episodes failed per the preregistered missingness categories and were handled according to the exclusion rule (exclude a pair only when both paired runs were technical failures). After exclusions 141 complete pairs entered the primary analysis. Provider-call accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 156, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 147, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 9; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150, repair = 6.

Condition-level outcomes and contingency. Condition summaries (complete_pairs = 141): baseline_successes = 135 (baseline success rate = 0.9574468085106383); guarded_successes = 141 (guarded success rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table derived from per-pair outcomes is: n11 = 135 (both accepted), n10 = 6 (guarded accepted, baseline rejected), n01 = 0 (baseline accepted, guarded rejected), n00 = 0 (both rejected).

Inferential results. The preregistered confirmatory exact two-sided McNemar test yields p = 0.03125. Observed paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.04255319148936165. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the paired difference (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. These numeric results and test parameters are archived in the analysis artifacts and execution manifest [14].

Discordant-case diagnostics. The six discordant pairs (n10) are traceable in the archived per-episode validator traces. Reconciliation links repair-stage activity to these discordant pairs: stage_counts report repair = 6 and provider-call accounting shows 6 repair-stage condition counts; each discordant pair's trace shows sanitizer normalization and/or a single permitted repair converted a draft the baseline validator rejected into a guarded final candidate the validator accepted. Detailed per-episode traces are retained in the archive [14].

Sensitivity to technical failures. Treating the nine both-missing pairs (both runs failed) conservatively as failures yields baseline acceptance = 135/150 = 0.9000 and guarded acceptance = 141/150 = 0.9400. This sensitivity exercise is conservative and documented in the archived analysis artifacts [14].
sections.discussion:
Reconciling hypothesis wording and the formal estimand. The preregistration's natural-language H1 asserted that verifier-gating would reduce attacker success (fewer unsafe configurations accepted). The registered formal estimand, however, measured paired validator acceptance-for-deployment (guarded − baseline). These differ conceptually: an increase in acceptance under the formal estimand can reflect successful recovery of reparable but otherwise rejected drafts (benefit for operator rework) rather than a reduction in attacker success. Our observed guarded→higher acceptance (≈4.255 percentage points) arose because sanitizer normalization and bounded repair recovered drafts that the baseline validator rejected. Therefore the preregistered directional attacker-centric claim is not supported by these data unless paired with an independent semantic-safety oracle; we report and interpret the archived formal estimand explicitly and caution against conflating validator acceptance with attacker-centric safety without additional semantic tests.

Operational implications and repair–gate co-design. Within the synthetic setting, combining input sanitization and bounded automated repair with deterministic gating can reduce operator rework by converting invalid drafts into validator-accepted candidates. That operational benefit is conditional on (a) validator semantic coverage (what invariants are encoded), (b) repair scope and correctness guarantees, and (c) transparency of repair operations for operator review. The six discordant cases demonstrate the mechanism: each was associated with a single permitted repair that enabled acceptance. If repairs inadvertently mask adversarial manipulations, acceptance can be harmful; hence deployment requires explicit co-design of gating policies, repair bounds, and validator expressiveness.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes CLI grammar, required sequences, and protected-interface invariants but does not capture all dynamic protocol-level semantics; acceptance-for-deployment is therefore a partial proxy for operational safety. Internal validity: technical failures (18/300) reduced effective sample size; the preregistered exclusion rule was applied and a conservative sensitivity check reported. External validity: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini), a single validator implementation, and a synthetic intent bank; results may not generalize across vendors, CLI dialects, topologies, or adversary models. Conclusion validity: the absolute effect is small relative to a high baseline (ceiling effect); statistical detectability (p = 0.03125) does not imply broad operational impact without further semantic-safety assessment.

Reproducibility note and protocol deviation. The archived model configuration recorded temperature = null (unset); this is a protocol deviation because provider defaults can affect sampling. To preserve paired comparability the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single generation per pair) and recorded provider-call accounting in the reconciliation artifact. For deterministic reproduction we recommend explicitly setting temperature = 0 when re-executing the archived execution manifest. All execution, reconciliation, and analysis artifacts required to reproduce the reported numerical results are archived and cited as the execution manifest [14].

Recommendations. Execute the preregistered benign-control to estimate false-positive blocking; preregister an attacker-centric estimand that couples validator acceptance with an independent semantic-safety oracle or reachability tests; diversify generators and validators across vendors and CLI dialects; and fix sampling settings (temperature = 0) for deterministic reproduction. Each recommendation follows directly from the archived evidence and provider-call accounting in the execution manifest [14].
sections.conclusion: A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment on a synthetic adversarial intent bank found that template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair produced a small but statistically detectable absolute increase in deterministic-validator-accepted LLM-generated configurations under the archived formal estimand (paired difference = 0.04255319148936165; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]). Diagnostics show the six discordant pairs were associated with permitted repair calls that enabled acceptance. Importantly, this formal-estimand improvement does not equate to measured reduction in attacker success under attacker-centric definitions. The run is limited by synthetic scope, a single model/validator, and a protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature). Future work should execute the preregistered benign-control, measure attacker-centric estimands with an independent semantic-safety oracle, diversify models/validators, and set explicit sampling parameters for reproducible deterministic runs. All principal numbers and reconciliation claims above are supported by the archived execution and analysis artifacts; the execution manifest is the primary machine-verifiable archive and is cited below as [14].

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock under the archived master prompt (provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature discovery, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer-review cycles, and revision reported here were performed autonomously after the lock. Declared models/tools and orchestration: primary generator = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; orchestration adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: study cand-2026-03 was preregistered and archived prior to observing outcomes (preregistration archived; see execution manifest [14]). Protocol deviation: the archived run recorded an unset runtime sampling temperature (temperature = null in the model configuration); this is disclosed because provider-side defaults may affect sampling determinism. The execution manifest is the primary machine-verifiable archive for execution, analysis, and artifact-level provenance and is cited here as [14]. No human manually edited or corrected the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Synthetic task bank and intent templates — not real production traffic or operator logs; results may not generalize to field datasets.
Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation limit external validity across vendors, protocols, and model families.
Validator coverage constrained to encoded safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants); some protocol-level or dynamic runtime semantics are not represented.
Technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion (both-run failures = 9) was preregistered and applied.
Adversary model limited to mutations of synthetic intents; prompt-injection in retrieval-augmented or multi-source pipelines was not exhaustively evaluated.
A preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrasing differed from the registered formal estimand; results are reported and interpreted with respect to the archived formal estimand.
The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking claims are made.
